extracted.intended_audience: novelists, creative writers, and literary students studying the craft of the novel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating novels that emphasize the 'fantastic' (fantasy/parody/adaptation) and the 'prophetic' (songlike, universal voice) aspects of fiction; includes how to handle mythology, devices, voice, and reader expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merging magic and common sense (the true fantasist)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mark of the true fantasist — merge the kingdoms of magic and common sense by using words that apply to both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use language and images that operate in both the mythic and the mundane so the mixture 'comes alive.' Example: Norman Matson's handling of a wish where words apply to both realms. This technique animates the mixture rather than keeping the two planes separate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of realism, wittiness, charm, and mythology
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat fantasy themes with a mixture of realism, wittiness, charm and mythology; the mythology is most important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain an appropriate balance so the work neither collapses into mere whimsy nor becomes unbearably heavy. Example: Zuleika Dobson succeeds because of its blend of these qualities. Over- or under-emphasizing any one element will alter the tone and effectiveness of the fantasy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of supernatural devices (supernatural machines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Borrowed or created supernatural machines/devices must be used with care; entrusting a character to the wrong device is inept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and place supernatural devices so they support the tone and mythology; misuse can make the fantasy 'heavy or thin.' Consider how a device interacts with realism and the book's overall mythology before deploying it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody/adaptation as a source of mythology
rubrics_metrics.description: The fantasist may adopt an earlier work and use it as a framework or quarry for his own purposes (parody or adaptation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody/adaptation can jump-start writers who struggle to create original characters by giving them a ready-made pattern or mythology (examples: Fielding using Pamela; The Magic Flute as a mythic source). Be aware of the risk of a 'false start' where the work ends up serious and independent (Joseph Andrews). Use the borrowed mythology as scaffold, not as a straitjacket.

rubrics_metrics.name: Borrow existing mythologies for structural guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer can take an existing work or tradition (Mozart's world, the Odyssey) as the mythology that guides the novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides an organizing pattern and can enable ambitious experiments (e.g., Joyce using the Odyssey for Ulysses). Use the source as 'guide and butt'—it should inform but not rigidly constrain the novel's aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecy as a tone of voice (song) rather than literal foretelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophecy here is an accent in the novelist's voice — he proposes to sing; the strangeness of song will shock; concern is with tone and diction rather than forecasting events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the novelist's state of mind and the minutiae of style; prioritize the phrasing and musicality of prose over strict adherence to everyday realism. Expect that furniture of common sense may be broken or shifted by this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader qualities demanded by prophetic fiction: humility and suspension of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: The prophetic aspect demands two qualities: humility and the suspension of the sense of humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should set aside ironic detachment and be willing to accept the prophetic voice; otherwise they risk misreading or mocking the prophetic intent. Without humility the prophet's voice will seem absurd; humour can blind readers to the prophet's gravity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters capable of extension (prophetic extension)
rubrics_metrics.description: In prophetic fiction characters and situations stand for more than themselves; they 'expand to embrace' the universal — the part points back to the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create characters who, while remaining individuals, imply or summon larger human or metaphysical truths (example: Dostoevsky's Mitya vs George Eliot's Hetty). A prophetic character often becomes meaningful because of what it implies beyond immediate actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spasmodic / intermittent realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophetic fiction is spasmodically realistic: the prophet can be patiently accurate about small, concrete things while otherwise singing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise, often laborious detail (trials, staircases, whaling catalogues, a field of grass) at moments to anchor the work and make the prophetic passages more vivid. These little foreground details create 'roughness of surface' that draws reactions but contribute to a lasting smoothness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophetic voice should be songlike, not reflective or workmanlike
rubrics_metrics.description: A prophet 'does not reflect' and 'does not hammer away' — the mode is song, not deliberative talk or tool-driven workmanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overbearing philosophical reflection or excessive technical contrivance that converts lyric impulse into a merely workmanlike exercise. Joyce is offered as a caution: too 'workmanlike' undermines the prophetic 'song.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Orientation toward unity vs multiplicity (prophecy vs fantasy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophecy is oriented towards unity (a face towards unity), whereas fantasy 'glances about' and its confusion is fundamental rather than incidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the novel's aim is to suggest an overarching unity (prophetic) or to revel in shifting mythologies and multiplicity (fantasy). This choice will determine structure, tone, and the acceptability of incoherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of invocation in fantasy
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy can employ a 'freedom of invocation' that produces a beauty unattainable by serious literature — funny, charming, iridescent yet profound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use playful invocations, personifications, and mythic flourishes to achieve effects that serious realism cannot; balance humour and depth so the tone remains charming rather than merely flippant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false starts when shifting mode from parody to seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Parody/adaptation may become a false start if the author begins comic pastiche but drifts into a serious independent work (Fielding's Joseph Andrews example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of tonal drift; if you borrow a mythology for comic effect, ensure the aim stays coherent or consciously allow a deliberate transformation into something else with attendant structural adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess novelist suitability for prophetic approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all novelists are fit for the prophetic aspect; the prophet is in a remoter emotional state while composing and avoids reflective philosophical hammering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether your temperament and aims suit prophecy: if your voice tends toward anxious problem-solving, survey-like breadth, or many reminiscences (examples: Hawthorne, Hardy, Conrad), the prophetic mode may not serve you. Prophecy requires a capacity for song and occasional abandonment of ordinary critical apparatus.
